title: Behavioral Detection of External Website Defacement across Platforms
shortTitle: Behavioral Detection of External Website Defacement acros...
summary: This strategy detects T1491.002, External Defacement, where an adversary alters the content of a public facing website, web application, or cloud hosted site to carry an unauthorised message. The value of the detection is damage control: the faster the altered content is found, the shorter the public exposure and the smaller the reputational cost. Detection blends file integrity monitoring on web document roots, web server access records for the upload or edit requests that changed content, and content management system audit logs for administrative edits. The main failure mode is alert fatigue from plugin updates, theme deployments, and caching layers, so the rule must separate a controlled release from an unexpected write.

beginner.definition: Defacement means someone changes a public website so it shows their own message or image. This detection watches the files and pages that make up a public site. It catches unauthorised content changes quickly.
beginner.whyItMatters: A defaced page is visible to every customer and to the press. The longer it stays up, the more trust is lost. The change may also be a side effect of a wider intrusion, so it is a useful warning sign. Finding it in minutes instead of days decides how the incident is reported.
howItWorks: A monitoring agent takes a fingerprint of every file in the website folder.
It compares the fingerprints on a schedule and reports any that changed.
The web server also logs each page request, including upload and edit actions.
The rule links a content change to the account and address behind the request.
Changes made outside a release window or by an unexpected account score higher.
The alert goes to your security information and event management (SIEM) platform and the web team.
beginner.example: Think of a shop window painted with the daily specials. A staff member repaints it every morning before opening, which is normal. If the window is repainted at three in the morning by someone nobody recognises, the picture itself is the same kind of paint. Only the timing and the identity of the painter tell you that something is wrong.
takeaways: File fingerprints on the web folder give you the earliest possible warning.
Pair the changed file with the request that changed it to learn who did it.
Publish a release calendar so that planned changes can be filtered out safely.

objectives: Explain what external defacement is and how it is normally discovered
Describe how file integrity monitoring detects content changes on a web server
Correlate a content change with the web request, account, and source address behind it
Use release windows and change records to separate planned updates from defacement
List the first response steps for a public website content change
dataSources: File integrity monitoring events from the web document root including file path, hash change, and modifying account
Web server access logs recording POST and PUT requests with the authenticated user, source address, and user agent
Content management system audit logs recording page, template, and media edits with the editor account
Sysmon event 11 file creation events on web servers for new files written under the site directory
Cloud storage access logs for static site hosting buckets recording object overwrite operations
logic: The pattern is content under a public web root changing without a matching authorised release. The rule selects file integrity events for the site directory and object overwrite records for static hosting, then joins them with web server or content management audit entries for the same paths within a short window, carrying the acting account and source address. The malicious case shows many files changed in one burst, changes outside the release calendar, edits by an account with no publishing role, or writes coming from an unexpected address or a scripted user agent. The benign case shows a deployment pipeline account changing files inside a scheduled window with a matching change record.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Web Root Content Changed Outside Release Window
# logsource:
#   product: linux
#   service: fileintegrity
# detection:
#   selection:
#     TargetPath|startswith:
#       - '/var/www/html/'
#       - '/srv/site/'
#     Action: 'modified'
#   filter_release:
#     User|endswith: 'svc-webdeploy'
#   condition: selection and not filter_release | count() by User > 10
# level: high
falsePositives: Content editors publishing articles and images through the approved management interface during working hours
Plugin, theme, and framework updates applied automatically by the hosting platform
Cache and thumbnail generation that writes derived files into subdirectories of the web root
Marketing campaigns that schedule page and banner changes using a service account outside core hours
tuningNotes: Exclude derived directories such as cache, uploads, and thumbnails, and allowlist the deployment service account only when the change falls inside a scheduled release window, so that a compromised deploy account still alerts outside those hours. Baseline the normal number of changed files per release so you can require a burst threshold before alerting, which removes single-file editor noise. Scope strict alerting to the production site and keep staging in review only. The coverage you lose is a slow single-page defacement inside an allowlisted directory, so add a daily hash comparison report for critical pages regardless of the alerting rule.
